tn.translation: Stress in Zialo is of the dynamic type, fixed, and falls mostly on the last syllable of the root. Stress is not distorted by tone or by vowel length ... Tone in Zialo is a phonological (meaning-distinguishing) category and plays a most important role in the morphosyntactic system. ... Two level tones are distinguished in Zialo: high and low. The bearer of tone is the vowel. The segmental base of tone is not the syllable but the metrical foot, which in general corresponds to the word. ... A super-high tone has so far been noted only on the conjunction hã̋ 'until'.
tn.cite: Бабаев, К. В. 2011. Фонологический и морфосинтаксический профиль языка зиало. Вопросы филологии 2011, № 3 (39): 37–51.

tn.note: Two level tones (H, L); a super-high noted on one conjunction only. Tone domain stated as the metrical foot (~word); much grammatical tone; fixed root-final stress said to be independent of tone.

5131.prule: No positional rule stated by the dedicated description. Ivanow 1935 p. 48: the accent is 'fairly mobile', does not follow the Literary Persian (LP) final-stress rule, and is on the first syllable 'only in some verbal forms'; it is realised by a mix of pitch raising and lengthening 'depending on intonation'. Morphological accent-attractors are named piecemeal: the definite suffix -é 'attracts the accent upon itself' (p. 60), the preverb bar 'is emphatic, attracting the accent' (p. 72), the durative prefix e- 'is stressed, and pronounced as i-' 'sometimes in YG, and almost always in KG' (p. 83) but under emphatic future meaning 'receives some stress... (it does not attract the accent upon itself, however)' (p. 79), LP-style bi- in biure/biwre 'is sharply accented' (p. 83), and the 3sg ending -uné has é 'semi-accented (as the real accent rests on the word itself)' (p. 85). The only fixed-position statements are the Dari Language Project parentheticals: 2003 Preliminary Report '(stress is always on the first syllable of the word)', narrowed by the same authors in the 2003 Summary of Findings to '(stress in Dari is always on the first syllable of a verb)'; both are asides inside a clitichood argument, and the authors' own accented forms m-e-t-ɑ́ 'he gives it to me' and e-vɛ́n-ɑ 'he throws it to us' (verb word beginning with the unstressed continuous prefix e-, which they call a verbal affix) contradict the literal verb-word-initial reading. 5133.tone: Tone language. Li 1977 §1.5.5 'Tones' (Lungchow): 'There are six tones in Lungchow: 1. mid level 33 2. mid falling from mid to low 31 3. high level 55 4. low level 11 5. rising from mid-low to mid-high 24 6. low falling from mid-low to low 21' (two-column list; the Google scan serves item 6's label after item 5's), 'The sixth tone is always accompanied by a glottal stop'; and 'Lungchow divides its syllables into two types: those that end in a vowel or a nasal, and those that end in a stop consonant (except the glottal stop, cf. supra). The first type may have any of the six tones, but the second type only two - tone 3, namely the high level tone 55, or tone 2, namely the mid falling tone 31.' On stress Li says only (§1.5.8) that the dialect 'does not have a strong contrast between different stresses' and that no specific study has been made of its stress patterns or of its intonation; he does not deny stress outright, so the record is tonal rather than no-word-stress. 5134.dq: Such syllables do not occur on the final edge of a word and may be derived through shortening of syllables in weak prosodic positions; in these iambic languages that is the initial edge of a prosodic foot.
5134.prule: Tone language, no stress rule. Lawngtlang Zophei is analysed with an underlying H vs. L vs. toneless contrast on every syllable (surface L, M, H and falling HM/ML, plus derived rises). Word prosody is described structurally as iambic sesquisyllables: one or more reduced 'minor' syllables (Ca, [ə], shorter, reduced contrasts) sit in the weak position, the initial edge of the prosodic foot, and the full 'major' syllable is the prominent one; minor syllables never occur at the final edge of a word/prosodic phrase, so the prominent major syllable is final in a sesquisyllable. No 'stress falls on syllable X' statement and no contrastive stress is claimed for Zophei.
5134.quote: [p.141] Minor syllables (or semi-, reduced, or pre-syllables) are similar to the Vʔ rhymes discussed above in that they are shorter and often offer fewer contrasts than major syllables. Such syllables do not occur on the final edge of a word and may be derived through shortening of syllables in weak prosodic positions; in these iambic languages that is the initial edge of a prosodic foot. [p.222] LTZ is analyzed in terms of an underlying H vs. L vs. toneless distinction on all syllables. 5134.exq_: In LTZ, tone is not predictable from syllable structure, and minor syllables can surface with L, M, or H pitch, as in the following words: tlà sah ‘let boil,’ ra møø ‘bamboo,’ and rá lɨɨ ‘ocean.’
5134.tone: Zophei is a tone language: 'LTZ is analyzed in terms of an underlying H vs. L vs. toneless distinction on all syllables' (p.222); tone is lexical on morphemes ('Underlying H tone morphemes are those which never surface as L; underlying L tone morphemes are those which never surface as H; and underlying toneless morphemes are not limited in their surface pitch', p.222). The only prominence statement is structural: the sesquisyllable is an iamb, weak minor syllable(s) + strong major syllable, minor syllables barred from the final edge (pp.141, 237); the author says it is 'not often clear whether contouring is licensed by the final edge or the prominent syllable' since they coincide (p.247). Unlike Hakha Lai/Lemi, LTZ minor syllables keep an L/M/H pitch contrast and a major syllable shortened to a minor one keeps its tone (bèh + tsih -> bà tsih, p.239). The word 'stress' is never applied to Zophei in the dissertation; the only 'accented on the last' line (p.233, p.215) is Stilson 1866 quoted on Khimi/Mro. The family-level companion paper (Lotven et al. 2020, JSALL 6(2), p.15) says 'In sesquisyllabic words, a stressed "major syllable" is preceded by a short, unstressed C or CV "minor syllable"... resulting in an iambic (unstressed-stressed) word structure' -- a Kuki-Chin generalisation, not a Zophei-specific rule.

tn.quote: In contrast, ꞌBëlï has three underlying level tones, evidenced by the number of tone melodies with the same syllable structure. Contour tone consists of more than one level tone on the same syllable. The syllable is the tone-bearing unit. ... The number of melodies in CV and CVCV syllable structure is evidence of a system with three underlying level tones. If there were only two underlying level tones, there would be no more than four contrastive tone melodies in any one word syllable structure.

5151.cfw: Nothing describes the prosody of Dongo Kresh itself: the record extrapolates Tucker & Bryan's (1966) remark for the Bongo-Bagirmi group as a whole that stress normally falls on the first syllable of disyllables (always so when the final vowel is reduced), while the only Kresh-specific account, Struck (1918) on a different, southern Kresh variety, states that no main or secondary accent can be distinguished and that the apparent stem-syllable prominence is an artefact of final-vowel reduction; Boyeldieu & Nougayrol (2008) and Boyeldieu (2020) say nothing about stress.

5152.heavy: Not applicable: no Parji rule is stated. The family-level sources split: Krishnamurti 2003 p. 27 gives initial stress 'short or long' (quantity-insensitive) but reports Telugu as weight-sensitive on p. 59; Sjoberg 1971 p. 22 gives automatic stress on initial syllables and on syllables 'containing long vowels or ending in a consonant'.
5152.prule: No reached source states a stress rule for Parji/Duruwa. The only Parji grammar (Burrow & Bhattacharya 1953, ch. I 'Orthography and Phonology' pp. 1-8) is silent: 0 hits for stress/accent/prominence/intonation/pitch in both OCRs, re-checked in stage C. The quoted Krishnamurti 2003 p. 27 sentence is a Dravidian-wide generalisation ('in any of the Dravidian languages'), hedged 'Normally' (initial syllable, 'short or long', non-phonemic); it names no language, and the same book reports a weight-sensitive pattern for Telugu (sec. 2.4.1, p. 59, excerpt: 'The stress falls on the first syllable if it is short; it falls on the second syllable which follows a short syllable and if it has a long vowel'), so it cannot be transferred to Parji as a fixed quantity-insensitive rule. Family-level default, for labelling only: initial stress (Krishnamurti 2003 p. 27; Zvelebil 1970 sec. 1.10.10 p. 40, 'the primary stress always on the first, i.e. radical, syllable'; McAlpin 1981 excerpt 'stress on the initial syllable of a word'), against weight-sensitive family-level variants in Sjoberg 1971 p. 22 ('Stress occurs automatically on the initial syllable of words and on syllables containing long vowels or ending in a consonant') and Steever 1998 (IA full-text fragments: 'Stress occurs in many Dravidian languages, but is not distinctive. Typically, stress falls on'; Brahui 'Long vowels attract stress').

5152.quote: The favoured syllable pattern of the word (free form) in Dravidian is (C)V̄CV/(C)VCCV/(C)VCVCV (three morae each). The other types are infrequent. There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants.
